<reason>B won the comparative policy clash. A established environmental harms and plausible coordination benefits, but did not adequately show that targeted withdrawals outperform charges and opt-in rules once substitution impacts and recurring operating costs are counted. B answered the pressure questions directly and explained why passing charges to consumers preserves incentives rather than defeating them. A’s claims that comparable schemes uniformly succeed and pricing merely funds cleanup were insufficiently grounded. Its closing also misrepresented B’s conditional acceptance of justified phase-outs as conceding that A’s proposed targets satisfied those conditions.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B’s strongest rebuttal dismantled “exit once”: outsourcing washing and collection does not eliminate recurring costs, and removing the original container does not necessarily reduce total environmental harm. This directly undercut A’s central contrast between temporary adjustment and permanent waste.</best_rebuttal>
